storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — skies are sunny, radar is clear and there is no thunderstorm fuel in the air, so the cove gets the same quiet, cooling evening as the surrounding towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's cooling effect is weak and fading: the 64°F water is about 6°F cooler than the air at 4 PM, drops under the ~5°F protective threshold around 5 PM, and by 7 PM the air is as cool as the water — moot tonight with nothing on radar.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: a quiet, dry northwest flow covers the area. The 3:52 PM radar scan showed no rain or storm cells anywhere in range, the model has essentially zero storm fuel (the instability measure forecasters call CAPE is 0–10 through the evening), and the National Weather Service forecast is simply “Sunny”, high near 72°F with a northwest wind around 8 mph. Stations around the cove are reading 68–72°F with no rain in the past hour.

Local effect — neutral: on storm days the cool Sound can lay a stable layer of air over the water that weakens incoming storms, but it needs the air to be at least about 5°F warmer than the water. At 4 PM that gap is only about 6°F (air near 70°F over 64°F water), which is weak. It also does not last: the Sound holds its temperature while the air cools toward sunset (6:18 PM), so the gap slips under 5°F around 5 PM, is about 2°F by 6 PM, and by 7 PM the air is slightly cooler than the water. There is no sea breeze today either — every coastal station is reading northwest, off the land.

Most likely outcome for the cove: dry and clear through the evening, with temperatures sliding from about 70°F at 5 PM to the low 60s by 7 PM and the northwest breeze fading. No difference between the cove and inland towns — there is nothing for the Sound to help or hurt.

Other things to know: the National Weather Service has a Coastal Flood Statement out for tomorrow (Tuesday) from noon to 3 PM — minor flooding of the most vulnerable low-lying shoreline spots is possible around the midday high tide. That is a tide issue, not a storm.

What would change the call: very little tonight. The NWS forecast discussion keeps most of the region dry, with only a stray shower or isolated thunderstorm possible well to the east (toward Groton) at night. The next real storm chance it flags is a strong frontal system on Friday, which could bring thunderstorms followed by strong winds and much colder air over the weekend; forecasters rate confidence in strong storms as low for now.

wind.tactics_blurb: A puffy northwest breeze off the land is running out of steam — about 6 kt at 5 PM, down to drifting conditions by sunset, then a light westerly. Stay in the middle of the course, sail to the puffs, and expect the slow trend to be left as the wind backs toward the west; the best racing is the first half hour.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of wind day: a light gradient wind — the breeze comes from the large-scale weather pattern, and no sea breeze is in play. The land is about 6°F warmer than the 64°F Sound (the air–water temperature difference a sea breeze needs is roughly 5°F, so this is marginal), but a sea breeze never formed: none of the 18 coastal stations shows a southerly, and all of them are northwest, blowing off the land. The well-sited airport anemometers average about 8 kt, right at the line between light and moderate, and the model has the wind fading through the window — so this is treated as a light-wind evening.

Through the window: at 4 PM Riverside Yacht Club was reading north-northwest (331°) at 11 kt, averaging 9 kt over ten minutes and gusting 14. From there it winds down: about 6 kt from the northwest at 5 PM, only 2–3 kt around 6 PM as the land cools toward sunset at 6:18 PM, then a light 3–4 kt westerly after dark. A gradient wind normally holds through sunset, but this one is weak enough that the evening cooling cuts the surface off from the wind above. Model data stops at 7 PM in this run, so the 8–10 PM rows carry the 7 PM wind forward and should be read as estimates.

Model versus the cove: the model is running behind the real wind. For 4 PM it had west-northwest (300°) at 6 kt, while the cove and Bridgeport both show north-northwest (330–340°) at about 10 kt — roughly 20–30° further right and 3–4 kt stronger. The 5 PM row is nudged up and to the right to reflect that; if the breeze keeps over-performing, expect a knot or two more than the table early in the window. This is a gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day, so the sea-breeze direction correction does not apply.

Where the pressure is and how it shifts: a northwest wind reaches the cove over trees and houses, so it comes in puffs with holes between them and swings 15–30° either side of the average. No side pays reliably — the best average pressure is in the middle of the cove, away from the lee of the western shore. Tack on the big headers and connect the puffs. The slow underlying trend is to the left, from about 320° at 5 PM to due west by 7 PM; a westerly tends to leave holes near the Connecticut shore with more breeze further out.

What it feels like: pleasant light-to-medium dinghy racing for the first half hour (6 kt with puffs near 10), then a drifter — under 4 kt from about 6 PM on, where a race committee may shorten course or abandon. Sunny and about 70°F at 5 PM, cooling to the low 60s by 7 PM, and dark after sunset.

data_caveats: HRRR model run only reached 7 PM (forecast hours 5–12 unavailable) — the 8, 9 and 10 PM wind rows are carried forward from the 7 PM value, not model output.
Model is running behind the real wind: it had west-northwest 6 kt for 4 PM while Riverside YC read north-northwest 11 kt — the 5 PM row is adjusted toward the observations.
Gust figures are estimates scaled from sustained wind and current station gusts — the model feed has no gust field.
Wind-regime call is borderline: airport stations average 8 kt, right at the light/moderate line; called light because the wind is forecast to fade through the window.
Western Long Island Sound buoy 44040 reading is 75 minutes old; water temperature is from Bridgeport Harbor.
Wind sensors down at Groton, Islip and Westhampton Beach airports — not used.
